segments.text: CSS/PMS Group III Optional Subject — Code 22, 100 marks

Business Administration is the study of how an organization is planned, staffed, financed, operated, and marketed so that it can achieve its purpose efficiently and effectively. The subject is built from five connected pillars, each answering a different question about how an enterprise functions:

items.text: Management
answers who decides, and how? — it is the process of planning, organizing, leading, and controlling people and resources toward common goals.
Human Resource Management (HRM)
answers who does the work, and how are they managed? — it covers acquiring, developing, motivating, and retaining the people who carry out the organization’s plans.
Financial Management
answers where does the money come from, and where does it go? — it covers raising capital, valuing it over time, and deciding which investments and financing choices create value for owners.
Operations and Supply Chain Management

answers how is the work actually done, and how do materials and information flow? — it covers designing processes, managing capacity and inventory, and coordinating the network of suppliers and distributors that gets a product or service to the customer.
Marketing
answers who is the customer, and how is value created and communicated to them? — it covers understanding needs, designing offerings, pricing them, and communicating and delivering value.

segments.text: These five pillars are not independent silos. A pricing decision (Marketing) affects cash flow (Finance); a capacity decision (Operations) affects hiring needs (HRM); a strategic decision (Management) sets the direction that every other function must support. Throughout this chapter, cross-references point out where one pillar’s decision constrains or enables another’s.

Read Management first, since its vocabulary (planning, organizing, leading, controlling; strategy; structure) is used throughout the other four pillars. Then HRM and Marketing, which are conceptually lighter and build intuition. Save Financial Management’s numerical topics (time value of money, CAPM, WACC, capital budgeting) for last, once you are comfortable with the underlying logic of “value” and “return” introduced earlier in the chapter, and expect to need worked practice, not just reading, for those topics.

Richard L. Daft’s Management, Stephen P. Robbins and Mary Coulter’s Management, Gary Dessler’s Human Resource Management, Ross, Westerfield & Jordan’s Essentials of Corporate Finance, Heizer & Render’s Operations Management, Chopra & Meindl’s Supply Chain Management, and Kotler & Armstrong’s Principles of Marketing are the standard textbooks behind this syllabus. Use them as reference works to deepen a specific concept, not as a cover-to-cover reading obligation — the official FPSC syllabus, not any one textbook’s table of contents, is the actual checklist for the exam.

items.text: Robbins, S. P., & Coulter, M. — Management (Pearson).
Daft, R. L. — Management (Cengage).
Mintzberg, H. — The Nature of Managerial Work (Harper & Row) — original source of the ten managerial roles framework.
Fayol, H. — General and Industrial Management — original source of the four (originally five) management functions.
Dessler, G. — Human Resource Management (Pearson).
Ross, S. A., Westerfield, R. W., & Jordan, B. D. — Essentials of Corporate Finance (McGraw-Hill).
Heizer, J., & Render, B. — Operations Management (Pearson).
Chopra, S., & Meindl, P. — Supply Chain Management: Strategy, Planning, and Operation (Pearson) — standard source for the strategic-fit and bullwhip-effect material in Unit IV.
Kotler, P., & Armstrong, G. — Principles of Marketing (Pearson).
Lewin, K. — original source of the three-step (unfreeze–move–refreeze) model of planned change, referenced in Unit I.

segments.text: Note on sourcing: the concepts, frameworks, and named models in this chapter (Fayol’s functions, Mintzberg’s roles, Katz’s skills, Porter’s generic strategies, Maslow’s hierarchy, Herzberg’s two-factor theory, Vroom’s expectancy theory, Lewin’s change model, CAPM, WACC, EOQ, and the bullwhip effect) are long-established, widely taught frameworks covered in the standard textbooks listed above. Numerical examples in this chapter are illustrative worked calculations constructed to demonstrate the underlying formulas, not reported findings from a specific study.
